description: We are passionate about healthcare innovation 🏥, human space exploration , astronaut health 🧑‍🚀, and technology-driven solutions 💡. Our skills include clinical assessment and health monitoring 🩺, research 🔬, critical thinking and problem-solving 🧩, teamwork 🤝, communication and visual storytelling 🎨, creative thinking, UI/UX and digital design 🖥️, and creating engaging presentations 📊. We aim to combine science, creativity, design, and technology to develop innovative, user-centered solutions for future space missions 🌌.
summary: VITALX is a flexible health-monitoring software engine for astronauts, built by NovaCare, a university team of three nurses and two programmers. It is not tied to one device: the same engine can run inside a smartwatch, a phone, a spacecraft computer, or a doctor dashboard, and it accepts data from any source that sends a timed reading, such as body-worn sensor patches, a watch, spacesuit and garment sensors, and cabin sensors (CO2, temperature, humidity, radiation). Each astronaut gets a personal profile: VITALX learns that person's own 14-day baseline, so it judges each body against itself instead of one fixed limit for everyone. Fixed limits alert only after a value is crossed, so slow drift goes unnoticed. VITALX validates the data, removes faulty readings, tracks slow drift, shows the trend with a stated margin of error, and sends one clear alert with its reason. A Smart Advisor then suggests what changed, what could happen, and what to do, while the crew physician makes the final decision. We tested it on real NASA OSDR environmental data from the RR-12 mission: 11,785 readings (35,355 values), of which validation removed 2,286 stuck values. In a sensitivity test with a slow synthetic CO2 drift added on top of the real RR-12 data, VITALX flagged it 6 days before the fixed limit. Vital signs are simulated because astronaut medical data is not public. VITALX runs fully offline; our prototypes run on a watch, a phone, and a doctor dashboard.
details:
Who we are: NovaCare is a university team of three nurses and two programmers. The nurses bring clinical experience in watching patients change slowly over time; the programmers turned that experience into software.

What it does: VITALX is an early-warning health engine for astronauts. It builds a personal baseline for every crew member and detects slow, gradual changes in vital signs and cabin conditions days before a fixed threshold is crossed. It then explains the reason and suggests next steps, and the crew physician decides.

One engine, any platform: VITALX is a software engine, not a single gadget. We designed it as a system that can be built into whatever the mission already uses:

- Inside a smartwatch or wristband worn by the astronaut.

- Inside a phone or tablet carried by the crew.

- Inside the spacecraft or station computer, watching the whole crew at once.

- Inside a ground or onboard doctor dashboard.

The core logic is the same everywhere. Only the screen changes, so the crew gets the same alert on the watch, on the tablet, and on the doctor's screen.

Any data source: VITALX treats every input as a channel: a timed value from a known sensor. Any source that can send that can be connected through a small adapter, without changing the engine:

- Body-worn sensor patches (heart rate, skin temperature, activity).

- Watch and wristband data (heart rate, sleep, steps).

- Spacesuit and smart-garment sensors during spacewalks and daily work.

- Spacecraft cabin sensors (CO2, temperature, humidity).

- Radiation dosimeters (daily and total dose).

We already connected real NASA OSDR cabin data this way through a NASA EDA adapter.

A personal profile for each astronaut: Every body reacts differently to space. A heart rate that is normal for one astronaut can be a warning sign for another. VITALX gives every crew member a personal profile and learns their own normal from their first 14 days, then compares each new reading with that person's own baseline, not with an average person.

How it works:

1) Collect: Receives data from any connected source: body sensors, watch, suit, and cabin.

2) Validate: Removes stuck sensor values, sudden spikes, and transmission gaps before anything is judged, so a broken sensor does not cause a false alarm.

3) Learn: Builds a personal baseline for each astronaut from the first 14 days.

4) Detect: Uses cumulative-change tracking (CUSUM) to catch slow drift that a fixed limit misses, while the fixed limit still catches sudden spikes.

5) Project: Shows where the trend is heading, with a stated margin of error rather than a fixed prediction.

6) Alert and advise: Sends one prioritized alert that shows each factor's share (for example CO2 52%, sleep 48%). The Smart Advisor then shows what changed, what could happen, and what to do, as suggestions only. The crew physician always makes the final decision.

What makes VITALX different:

- Earlier warning: it catches slow drift days before a fixed limit is crossed. In our RR-12 sensitivity test, it was 6 days earlier.

- Personal, not one-size-fits-all: every astronaut is compared with their own baseline.

- Platform-agnostic: one engine runs on a watch, a phone, a spacecraft computer, or a dashboard.

- Open to any sensor: new data sources plug in through adapters, including suits and garments.

- Works with fixed limits, not against them: fixed limits catch sudden spikes, and VITALX catches slow drift. Across 10 real NASA missions, each method was first in different cases, so we use both.

- Explains every alert: the crew sees why, not just a red light.

- Fully offline: built for deep-space missions with long communication delays, where the doctor on Earth may answer minutes later.

- Safe by design: suggestions only, no automated treatment, and a human always decides.

Benefits and impact: Gives crew members and flight surgeons days of lead time instead of reacting after a limit breach. It is designed to reduce alert fatigue by sending one prioritized alert instead of many, and it helps astronauts take responsibility for their own health on long missions, as the challenge asks.

Tools: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript (installable offline Progressive Web App with a Service Worker), Android application (smartwatch and phone prototypes), Firebase for event logging, JavaScript (Node.js) for NASA OSDR data processing, and GitHub Pages for hosting. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an AI assistant for code and text drafting, with all outputs reviewed and verified by our team.

Creativity: Replaces rigid, one-size-fits-all thresholds with an adaptive personal engine that can live on any device and read any sensor. Every alert explains its contributing factors and gives decision support rather than automated intervention.

Factors we considered: Data transparency (real NASA cabin data paired with clearly labelled simulated astronaut vitals), medical safety (a human always decides, with no automated treatment), offline reliability, flexibility across devices and sensors, and a clean, icon-first interface designed for high-stress environments.
